Kim Wilson, the former finance director for the City of Prichard, Alabama, has pleaded not guilty to theft charges, according to WKRG News 5. Wilson turned herself in to the Mobile County Sheriff's Office on Friday, marking the first court appearance in what appears to be a financial misconduct case involving the city's finance department.

Details surrounding the specific allegations remain limited at this stage, though the case involves potential misappropriation of city funds. The timing of Wilson's surrender suggests the investigation had been ongoing before formal charges were filed.

This development comes as Prichard continues to manage its financial operations. The case is now in the court system, with Wilson's not guilty plea setting the stage for further legal proceedings.

item.title: Congressman Patronis Comments on Meta Settlement, Jelly Roll, Carrier Renaming and More
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Congressman Jimmy Patronis joined Pensacola's Morning News on Monday for a conversation that ranged from social media regulation to Navy shipbuilding to a country music controversy that's got Northwest Florida talking. Meta's Settlement and Kids Online Patronis says Meta's recent $1.8 billion settlement over child…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Congressman Jimmy Patronis joined Pensacola's Morning News on Monday for a conversation that ranged from social media regulation to Navy shipbuilding to a country music controversy that's got Northwest Florida talking.


Meta's Settlement and Kids Online

Patronis says Meta's recent $1.8 billion settlement over child safety concerns is really just the company admitting it has a problem — but he doesn't think the dollar amount comes close to forcing real change. Spread over ten years, he points out, it works out to about $180 million a year, which he says is smaller than Escambia County's annual budget. He's backing a Section 230 reform bill that would hold social media companies responsible for predatory content and late-night push notifications aimed at kids — and says he's found an unlikely ally in a Democratic member of Congress from California who told him the idea crosses party lines because everyone cares about protecting kids. Patronis also praised Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier's decision to reject Meta's settlement money in favor of pursuing tougher policy changes in court, comparing it to holding out for real accountability rather than a token payout.


Ford Class Carrier and the Doris Miller Question

Patronis defended President Trump's push to overhaul systems on the Navy's newest aircraft carrier class, including the electromagnetic catapult system that's had documented problems since it debuted. He says the Ford class has plenty of strengths, but its first real stress test revealed deficiencies worth fixing — and argues the president's public pressure campaign is really aimed at forcing a notoriously slow-moving Pentagon bureaucracy to act faster. On the more sensitive question of reportedly renaming the carrier currently honoring Doris Miller — a Black sailor awarded the Navy Cross for heroism at Pearl Harbor — after President Trump, Patronis said he didn't know enough about where those reports originated to comment on them directly.


Canada, Trade, and a Lake Named America

Patronis defended the president's proposal to rename Lake Ontario as leverage in trade negotiations with Canada, framing it as a deliberate irritant designed to keep Canadian officials talking and pressure their leadership. He compared it to other tactics the administration has used to extract concessions, pointing to steel tariffs as an example of a policy he says has genuinely helped American manufacturing jobs.


Jelly Roll

Patronis stood by his earlier comments suggesting Jelly Roll isn't welcome in Florida after the singer joked about President Trump during an appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live. He compared the backlash to the Dixie Chicks controversy from the early 2000s and said the singer misjudged an audience that skews conservative. He believes more of his Northwest Florida listeners are frustrated with Jelly Roll than defending him. Andrew McKay disagreed with the framing, arguing that criticizing a joke is different from suggesting someone shouldn't be welcome in the state over their viewpoint.


The National Debt

Asked about the national debt closing in on $40 trillion, Patronis said it matters and ties it to the broader push to rebuild the economy after COVID-era disruptions, though he acknowledged meaningful progress on the debt itself will be difficult within a single presidential term.


UWF Football

On a lighter note, Patronis and McKay closed out the conversation celebrating UWF's season-opening win over a nationally ranked opponent, with Patronis saying the Argonauts win has generated serious buzz on social media heading into their next matchup.

item.content:encoded:
Atmore is gearing up for the return of Patterson Street Fun Day, an annual community event now in its sixth year that brings together young people, families, and first responders in a celebration of positive relationships.

Hosted by EMJ Atmore Outreach, the event creates an informal setting where residents can connect with local law enforcement and emergency personnel outside of typical emergency situations. The focus on relationship-building between community members and first responders has become a hallmark of the annual gathering.

Patterson Street Fun Day reflects a growing trend across the region of using community events to strengthen ties between neighborhoods and the public servants who work there. For families in the Atmore area, it offers a chance to participate in activities while getting to know local officers and emergency workers in a relaxed environment.

Details on the specific date, activities, and other aspects of this year's Patterson Street Fun Day weren't immediately available, but the event typically draws significant participation from the Atmore community.

item.dc:creator: newsroom

The artwork was painted by Enrique Lopez, a graduate of Mobile County Schools, and serves as a visual tribute to the community's rich cultural heritage. The mural's unveiling marks another effort by…
item.content:encoded: The Mobile County Training School revealed a new mural Friday celebrating the school's historical ties to Africatown, according to school officials. The artwork was painted by Enrique Lopez, a graduate of Mobile County Schools, and serves as a visual tribute to the community's rich cultural heritage. The mural's unveiling marks another effort by the school to honor and preserve the legacy of Africatown, one of the most historically significant African American communities in the region. Africatown, founded by formerly enslaved people brought to the U.S. aboard the Clotilda slave ship, remains an important cultural landmark in Mobile and continues to draw recognition for its contributions to American history.

The Blue Wahoos will look to bounce back as they continue their push toward clinching a playoff position in the coming days.

item.title: Typical summer heat returns to Pensacola area this week

item.content:encoded:
North Escambia can expect temperatures climbing into the low 90s this week, with the best chances for rain hitting midweek, according to the National Weather Service forecast.

Monday will start mostly sunny with highs near 91 degrees and just a 30 percent chance of showers and thunderstorms after 1 p.m. Northeast winds around 5 mph will shift to the southeast during the afternoon. Monday night should cool to around 73 degrees with partly cloudy skies and a 20 percent chance of isolated showers before 10 p.m.

Forecasters say rain chances will peak by Wednesday and Thursday as moisture increases, so residents should keep an eye on the forecast if they have outdoor plans mid-week. The typical summer pattern of afternoon heat and scattered storms looks to continue through the period.

item.title: Gas Prices Edge Up To $3.89 As Labor Day Weekend Approaches
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Florida drivers heading into the Labor Day weekend will find slightly higher prices at the pump, with the state average for regular unleaded hitting $3.89 per gallon this week. That's a 3-cent jump from the previous week, according to AAA. While the uptick is modest, it continues a pattern that's held steady throughout the summer months. For…
item.content:encoded:
Florida drivers heading into the Labor Day weekend will find slightly higher prices at the pump, with the state average for regular unleaded hitting $3.89 per gallon this week. That's a 3-cent jump from the previous week, according to AAA.

While the uptick is modest, it continues a pattern that's held steady throughout the summer months. For Pensacola-area drivers planning holiday trips over the long weekend, the price hike is unlikely to dramatically change travel plans, but it's worth factoring into fuel budgets for extended drives to the beach or out of state.

AAA notes that despite weekly fluctuations, gas prices have remained relatively stable compared to price swings seen in previous years. Motorists looking to stretch their fuel dollars might consider filling up earlier in the week rather than waiting until the weekend when demand typically pushes prices higher.

item.content:encoded:

Keyunta Iveon Ewing, who goes by the nickname "Baby K," appeared before a judge Friday for the transfer hearing. He faces a first-degree murder charge stemming from the incident at the park.

The teen's case was moved from juvenile court to the adult system following the hearing. Ewing remains in custody without the possibility of bail as the case proceeds through the criminal justice system.

Details about the circumstances of the shooting and Ewing's defense claims were not immediately available. The case is ongoing.

item.title: Florida Cattle Ranchers Blast Trump's Beef Import Plan
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Florida's cattle ranching community is pushing back against President Donald Trump's announcement of a tariff-free beef import deal aimed at lowering consumer prices. Trump said the arrangement would bring in 300,000 tons of imported beef and reduce prices by as much as 25 percent, according to social media posts from the president. The plan has…
item.content:encoded:
Florida's cattle ranching community is pushing back against President Donald Trump's announcement of a tariff-free beef import deal aimed at lowering consumer prices. Trump said the arrangement would bring in 300,000 tons of imported beef and reduce prices by as much as 25 percent, according to social media posts from the president.

The plan has drawn criticism from local ranchers who argue the influx of foreign beef could undercut their own operations and livelihoods. While Trump blamed inflationary pressures from the Biden administration for the need to lower beef costs, ranchers contend that opening the market to massive imports isn't the answer.

The disagreement highlights a broader tension in agricultural policy: balancing consumer demand for affordable food with support for domestic farming and ranching operations. For Northwest Florida's cattle industry, the outcome of this policy dispute could have real economic consequences.
